# Why Fixing a Cheap Part Can Be an Expensive Problem

When a washing machine breaks, the natural instinct is to look up the price of the failed component. A water inlet valve costs twelve dollars. A door switch costs eight. A drive belt costs fifteen. From this, many owners conclude that repair should be quick and cheap—and they are often baffled when a repair quote comes back at $200, or when the technician recommends replacing the entire machine. The gap between the price of a part and the cost of a repair is one of the most misunderstood aspects of household appliance ownership. The story of a fictional machine, a "CleanCo 4000" front-loading washer, illustrates why.

## Diagnosis: Finding the Fault Is Half the Battle

Imagine the CleanCo 4000 refuses to spin. The drum fills, the pump runs, but the clothes come out sopping wet. The owner searches online and finds dozens of possible culprits: a worn door lock actuator, a failed motor
